Ad Hominem: the text attacks a person instead of arguing against the claims.
Ad Populum: the text affirms something is true because the majority thinks so.
Black-and-White Fallacy: the text presents two alternative options as the only possibilities yet more exist.
False Cause: the text assumes two correlated events must also have a causal relation.
Circular Reasoning: the text tries to prove a point by simply repeating the point in different words.
Deductive Fallacy: the text presents a conclusion that doesn’t logically follow from the premises.
Emotional Language: the text arouses non-rational emotions.
Equivocation: the text uses a key term in multiple senses, leading to ambiguous conclusions.Extension Fallacy: the text attacks an exaggerated version of the opponent’s claim.
Hasty Generalization: the text draws a broad conclusion based on a limited sample.
Intentional Fallacy: the text relies on the author’s intent instead of focusing on the meaning within the text itself.
Irrelevant Authority: the text cites an authority, but the authority lacks relevant expertise.
Red Herring: the text introduces an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the main argument.
